title: Should the Bible Be Taught in Public Schools, No
author: Joe Carter
summary: Joe Carter responds to the Texas State Board of Education's new statewide required reading list, which includes about a dozen Bible passages from second grade through senior year, by arguing that Christians should oppose Bible reading in public schools. His authority is J. Gresham Machen, the staunch defender of biblical authority who in 1933 said he was as opposed to Bible reading in state schools as any atheist. Carter advances three of Machen's reasons. First, the Bible is unlike any other book, yet the Texas curriculum folds passages into thematic groupings, such as pairing Matthew 6 with All Creatures Great and Small, that obscure their meaning and invite interpretive bias. Second, teaching Scripture for cultural literacy or character education trades the gospel for civil religion. Third, a 'garbled Bible is a falsified Bible': reciting Psalm 23 or the Lord's Prayer without the redemptive core teaches moralistic therapeutic deism. He closes charitably, granting that supporters want children to meet the most important book, but insists the task belongs to parents and the church rather than state curricula. Filed as Learning & Curriculum as a close call because the subject is a state curriculum mandate, though the reasoning is theological.
points: Texas's mandated list of roughly 200 works, taking effect in 2030-31, includes Bible passages embedded in thematic units alongside secular anchor texts.
Carter argues pairings like Matthew 6 with Herriot's animal stories steer students toward the secondary theme rather than the passage's central claim about trusting God.
He notes an inconsistency: people who distrust public school teachers' neutrality on history and science would entrust them with interpreting Scripture.
Following Machen, using Scripture for cultural literacy or 'character education' substitutes a generic civic religion for Christian faith.
The dividing question is not whether the Bible deserves a central place in children's formation but whether a state curriculum can give it that place.
quotes: Earlier this summer, the Texas State Board of Education approved a list of mandated texts, making it the first state in the nation to have a statewide required reading list. Out of the roughly 200 mandated works, about a dozen are Bible passages. The selections are spread from second grade through senior year of high school. The list takes effect starting in the 2030–31 school year.

Machen is worth hearing on this issue precisely because no one can accuse him of theological squishiness or embarrassment about the Bible. He gave his career, his reputation, and eventually his denominational standing to defend the full authority of Scripture. Why, then, did he so strongly oppose Bible reading in public schools?
Yet the way Texas plans to teach the Bible is to treat it as merely a part of Genre B—and not even the most important part.

Yet of the two competing messages—we should care about animals, and God cares about us—which are sixth graders likely to take from the reading, especially when it’s framed by the context of those other literary works?

Even if we were to set aside the problem of reading these passages in the context of other secular works, we still have the problem of unorthodox bias. As Machen points out, “The reading of the Bible is very difficult to separate from propaganda about the Bible.

It’s shocking that the same people who don’t trust public school teachers to teach history, literature, or science in a sufficiently unbiased way endorse having those same teachers teach interpretation of Scripture.

Using the words of Scripture—stripped of the requirement to see Jesus as Lord—to promote civics, character formation, or national heritage is a replacement of the biblical orthodox faith for generic civic religion.

The question that divides us isn’t whether the Bible deserves a central place in the formation of children—on that we agree—but whether a state curriculum is capable of giving it the place it deserves. Machen’s answer, and mine, is that it isn’t. We believe that the responsibility to teach God’s Word to children remains where God assigned it: with parents and with the church.
